messages.author: e54c74980a01d9ed
messages.subject: Question for using 85% CI
parts:
Hi all!

This may be a very simple question, but I notice in a lot of occupancy modeling papers that an 85% confidence interval is used as opposed to a 95% confidence interval that I feel like is more common. Can anyone explain why 85% is used here?

Thanks in advance!
Maria

messages.author: 38dd11f2eaa0b9d3
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Question for using 85% CI
parts:
Maria, 

It's been a few years since I read the paper, but I cited it in my thesis and avian occupancy publication in Forest Ecology and Management. Others can speak to the deeper statistical justifications (or lack thereof) for using 85% CIs in determining "uninformative parameters," but the Arnold (2010) paper forms the basis on which my use of the 85% CI was predicated. 

Arnold, T., 2010. Uninformative parameters and model selection using Akaike's Information Criterion. J. Wildl. Manag. 74, 1175–1178.

Dan Hannon

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Question for using 85% CI
parts:
That paper has the following:  "...investigators might consider using 85% confidence intervals so that model-selection and parameter-evaluation criteria are more congruent."

So if one lives and dies by AIC (and have read Arnold's paper), then maybe 85% is the way to go.  (Although if I understood the paper correctly,the congruence is about the 2 AIC units rule more closely matching conclusions with 85% confidence intervals.  If so, why not keep 95% and change the AIC rule?)

But if one has not taken into consideration the consequences/costs of either making a right or wrong decision, then I would stick with 95% as it is a common standard despite it being arbitrary.  Certainly in the past folks have used 80% (and 50%) because the smaller intervals give the appearance of more precision.  The best way to cause confusion is to use a variety of standards.  (In the distant past I've seen folks who go the other direction and want 99% confidence intervals to justify that their chemical processes were in control - their confidence intervals were so wide that it became nearly impossible to declare a process was out of whack.  And yet they claimed "More confidence!!" in their results.)

Jim

messages.author: 564e5c2fe0c2d390
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Question for using 85% CI
parts:
Hi Maria,

The quadratic form of variables is used to account for non-monotonic associations. For example, if detection probability was lower/higher on middle dates in relation to the beginning and ending of your sampling season, then you have a reason to include the quadratic form of date (remember to always include the linear form if you do, i.e., the quadratic form goes always with the linear form).

Best,

José.

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Question for using 85% CI
parts:
Many functions (but not all) can be approximated with a polynomial.  Going from linear (date) to quadratic (date squared) is just attempting to obtain a better approximation to an unknown function using a higher order polynomial.

For some it's a tough choice between "better approximations without interpretability" and "better interpretability without a great approximation".  I lean towards the former.

Jim
